# Seth Godin on Pricing: 'You Pay a Lot But Get More Than You Pay For'

**Source:** Seth Godin on Young and Profiting podcast, Oct 2026  
**Video:** https://www.youtube.com/live/l0VL1ljufqU  
**Duration:** 45 min  
**Captions:** English (auto-generated)

---

## The Core Insight

Seth articulates two competing pricing strategies:

1. **The Race to the Bottom** (or "Pick me because I'm cheaper")
   - Optimize for lowest cost
   - Compete on commoditization
   - Winner is the one who can operate at lowest margin
   - Fragile: any competitor with lower overhead beats you

2. **The Race to the Top** ("You'll pay a lot, but you get more than you pay for")
   - Optimize for perceived value
   - Compete on emotional labor, wisdom, insight
   - Winner is the one people would miss if they were gone
   - Resilient: hard to copy; builds moats

**The choice:** Pick one. Don't try to be both. "There are two choices you have to make when you're going to do your work. Either you say, 'You can pick anyone and I'm anyone. I'm cheaper.' Or you can say, 'You'll pay a lot, but you get more than you pay for.' That's the race to the top."

---

## Why This Matters

### The "Get What You Get" Principle (David Cross reference)

The pricing strategy maps onto the "get what you get" tattoo concept: if you're hiring for median ("just get me a body to do tasks"), you get commodity service. If you're hiring for excellence ("I need someone to smash it out of the park"), you need seniority and are willing to pay for it.

**In consulting:** €800/day is the market rate for a body. But if you're paying for seniority, expertise, pattern-breaking insight, you're in a different game entirely — and the person delivering it should be worth more than they cost.

### The Agent Problem

This principle is becoming *increasingly apparent* with agents and multitasking systems. You're paying a considerable amount, but you're getting way more than you pay for — because the agent can do things no individual consultant can do at that price point.

---

## Key Quotes

> "There are two choices you have to make when you're going to do your work. Either you say, 'You can pick anyone and I'm anyone. I'm cheaper. Pick me.' Or you can say, 'You'll pay a lot, but you get more than you pay for.' That's the race to the top. That's very hard to pull off. 'Cuz you have to do hard work to be worth more than you pay for. That's the place to go. That is a resilient strategy that works in almost every industry."

> "To be the one that we would miss if you were gone because you bring emotional labor and insight and wisdom to the work you do, and you're not looking for a shortcut."

## Application to Product/Service Pricing

**Race to the Top playbook:**

1. Don't compete on price. Ever. (You lose to someone cheaper.)
2. Compete on *irreplaceability*: emotional labor, wisdom, specific insight the buyer can't get elsewhere
3. Build for the people who say "I've been waiting for this" — not the people you have to convince
4. Price accordingly: if you're rare + valuable, charge rare + valuable prices
5. The hard part: actually being worth it. ("You have to do hard work to be worth more than you pay for.")
